HISTORY:
• Main complaint: Dry cough and constant nasal discharge started ~5 days ago.  
• Cough: Dry, occurs every 20-30 min; no sputum, no hemoptysis, no chest pain, no dyspnea, no pleuritic pain.  
• Nasal symptoms: Profuse “streaming” rhinorrhea with green discharge; no epistaxis, no sinus or facial pain reported.  
• Systemic/associated: Subjective fever with alternating chills; myalgias; transient diarrhea at onset (resolved); no vomiting, no rash, no headache, no visual changes, appetite and oral intake preserved, normal urine output.  
• Triggers/relievers: Lemsip (paracetamol-containing hot drink) 2-3 doses/day provides temporary throat relief.  
• No previous similar episodes mentioned.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Hypertension.  
• No chronic pulmonary disease noted.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies; mild seasonal hay fever.  
• Medications:  
  – Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Lisinopril – “200 mg” reported (dose appears inaccurate; conflict noted).  
• Social: Non-smoker status not documented; drinks alcohol “the odd sherry.” Lives with partner and dog; office manager.  
• Last diabetes blood test ~3 weeks ago reported “normal.” Blood pressure last checked “a while ago,” status unknown.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (video):
• Patient appears well, conversing in full sentences.  
• No observed respiratory distress.  
• Alert and oriented.  
• No visible rash.  
(Note: No vitals measured; no chest auscultation possible.)

IMPRESSION:
Likely viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) with possible early chest involvement; currently uncomplicated.

MANAGEMENT PLAN:
• Supportive care: Continue Lemsip (contains paracetamol); avoid additional paracetamol-containing products.  
• Symptom control: Daytime—no cough suppressants; nighttime—may use small amount of cough syrup if sleep-preventing.  
• Monitoring: Purchase a thermometer and check temperature regularly.  
• Red-flag advice: Re-contact GP/urgent care if temperature ≥37.5-38 °C persists or spikes, cough worsens, purulent sputum develops, hemoptysis, new chest pain, shortness of breath, or nasal bleeding.  
• Diabetes/HTN care: Maintain scheduled blood sugar and blood pressure reviews with GP.

PATIENT SUMMARY:
A 65-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presents with a 5-day history of dry cough and profuse rhinorrhea, consistent with a probable viral respiratory infection. No concerning respiratory or systemic features at present. She is advised on supportive measures, temperature monitoring, and warning signs that warrant reassessment.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Buy a thermometer and monitor temperature; seek care if fever persists or rises.  
• Continue Lemsip; do not take other paracetamol products simultaneously.  
• Return promptly if breathing difficulties, chest pain, or worsening/ purulent cough occurs.

NEXT STEPS:
• Self-monitor symptoms and temperature over the next 1–2 weeks.  
• Contact GP if red-flag symptoms develop or if no improvement within 14 days (possible need for antibiotics).  
• Arrange routine diabetes and blood pressure reviews as previously scheduled.

• Missing expected elements: Vital signs, smoking status confirmation, detailed medication doses/frequencies, recent BP readings, allergy verification.  
• Internal conflicts: Patient reports lisinopril “200 mg” (dose unusually high) – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional incomplete sentences but key clinical data obtainable.
